text: To dissuade someone is to talk them out of doing something — the exact opposite of persuade, which talks them into it. Visa worries and a political mood many foreigners read as unwelcoming dissuaded some international soccer fans from making the trip to America at all.

Rabid means extreme and fanatical — enthusiasm so intense it borders on out of control. (It literally describes an animal with rabies, which is where the wild, uncontrolled sense comes from.) The article says the Canadian and Mexican host cities have more rabid soccer fans — the kind who pack stadiums and cross countries for a match — and that's one reason their hotels are filling faster.
To outpace someone is to move faster than them — to pull ahead in a race. Here the race is hotel bookings, and Canada and Mexico are outpacing almost every American host city.

When a city “boasts” the top occupancy rates, nobody is bragging out loud — this sense of boast means to proudly possess something impressive. It's a favorite of travel and business writing: “the hotel boasts an infinity pool.”

A hotel's occupancy rate is the share of its rooms that are actually filled — 48% occupancy means about half the rooms are booked. It's the number the whole article turns on: it's how you measure whether World Cup visitors are really showing up.
To crack a threshold is to break through a level — the way you crack a code or crack the top ten. San Francisco is the only U.S. city to crack 40% booked; nothing is literally cracking.

A threshold is the line where something begins to count — originally the strip at the bottom of a doorway you cross to enter. Here it's the 40%-booked mark: cross it and your city looks like a real World Cup destination.

A counterpart is the matching version of something on the other side — the person or thing holding the same role in a different place. The “American counterparts” of Vancouver and Guadalajara are the U.S. host cities playing the same role in the tournament, just with emptier hotels.

The “political climate” has nothing to do with weather — climate here means the overall mood or atmosphere of a place and time. The article says many foreigners perceive America's current political climate as unwelcoming, and that feeling alone is keeping some fans away.

Not the credit card! A visa is the official permission a country stamps into your passport letting you enter. “Visa concerns” means fans worried they couldn't get that permission in time — or at all — so they never booked the trip.

To perceive something is to see or interpret it a certain way — and what people perceive can matter more than what's true. Whether or not America actually is unwelcoming, enough foreigners perceive it that way to change their travel plans, and hotels feel the difference either way.

An enthusiast is someone genuinely devoted to a hobby or interest — a fan with real commitment behind the excitement. The “international soccer enthusiasts” here are exactly the travelers U.S. host cities were counting on.

Aspirational comes from aspire, to reach for something above you. “Aspirational travelers” are fans for whom the World Cup trip was a dream at the edge of their budget — a stretch, not a sure thing. When ticket prices hit $20,000, those are precisely the people who get squeezed out first.

To be shut out of a marketplace is to be excluded from it entirely — the door closed in your face, usually by prices you can't pay. (In sports a shutout is when a team is held to zero, which carries the same flavor: you got nothing.)

At an airport, customs isn't “traditions” — it's the government checkpoint where officers inspect arriving travelers and their bags before letting them into the country. Worries about getting through U.S. customs, the article says, are deterring some World Cup visitors.

To be detained is to be held by the authorities — stopped and kept, whether for an hour of questioning or much longer. News stories about travelers being detained at U.S. borders have spooked would-be visitors, a hotel executive says.

To deter someone is to scare or discourage them out of doing something — fear doing the persuading. Concerns about airport customs are deterring some fans from visiting; it's the same root as “deterrent,” something that exists to keep people away.

Applied to numbers, modest means small — nothing to write home about. Pebblebrook expects only a “modest boost” from the matches: a little extra business, far short of the bonanza host cities dreamed of. (Of a person, modest means humble — same idea of not being big.)

To displace something is to push it out and take its spot. The World Cup guests largely displaced the regular summer visitors the hotel would have had anyway — so the rooms are just as full as usual, not fuller. That's why the tournament isn't the windfall it looks like.

When a business number is “flat,” it isn't deflated like a tire — it's unchanged, a line on a chart going neither up nor down. Occupancy is flat at the Miami hotel: World Cup or not, the same share of rooms is filled as in a normal June.

To count on something is to rely on it — to build your plans around it showing up. The hotel boss counts on regular summer business each year; other owners are still counting on a last-minute wave of bookings to save the tournament.

Nobody behind a wheel here: in business-speak, a driver is the force pushing a result. “Price is likely a big driver” means price is the main reason Mexico's cheap rentals are filling up first — around $100 a night versus $300 in Kansas City, Boston, and Miami.

Short-term rentals are homes and apartments rented by the night, Airbnb-style, instead of leased for months. They compete with hotels for the same travelers — and in Mexico they're booking fast because they're a third of the U.S. price.

Transient means passing through — staying only briefly. (It comes from the Latin for “crossing over.”) “Transient travelers” is hotel-industry language for ordinary individual guests booking a night or two, as opposed to big groups or business blocks.

To materialize is to actually appear — to go from possible to real, like a ghost taking solid form. The hotel CEO's hope rests on history: up to 40% of bookings materialize within six days of a match. The fans exist; the question is whether their reservations become real.

To attribute a result to something is to name it as the cause — to give it the credit or the blame. The travel executive attributed Mexico City's strong demand largely to Latin American fans traveling there, rather than to Americans heading south.

An American idiom that simply means “in Mexico” — the border being the U.S.–Mexico line. The luxury travel company has had “plenty of success south of the border” even as its U.S. business disappoints.

A trek is a journey on foot, often a long slog — the word comes from ox-wagon migrations across southern Africa. Calling the walk from downtown Toronto hotels to the stadium “an easy trek” is the point: no $98 train ticket required, unlike the ride from Manhattan to MetLife Stadium.

Something that is unfolding is happening gradually, revealing itself piece by piece — the image is of a folded map opening up. The tournament is “unfolding across 16 North American cities”: not one event in one place, but a story spreading out over a month and a continent.
Soccer's world governing body — the organization that runs the World Cup and decides which cities host it. The initials are French, for the International Federation of Association Football.
